scenario: On Black Friday, 20,000 open order-tracking screens each ask the API for the order's status every five seconds, and almost every answer is "no change".
stem: Why does this design hurt so much at peak?
options: Polling cost grows with the number of watchers times the poll frequency, regardless of how often orders actually change
Front Door caches every status response, so the API has to answer each request twice
Five-second polling opens a new WebSocket for every request, which exhausts the App Service instances
API Management cannot pass more than 1,000 requests a second to a single backend
explanation: 4,000 requests a second are generated by watchers alone, even when no order moves; push costs scale with changes instead. Polling does not open WebSockets at all, and the problem is the volume of pointless requests, not a fixed gateway ceiling.

scenario: Ana likes server-sent events for order tracking: it is one-way, plain HTTP and the browser reconnects on its own. All of the shop's public traffic goes through Front Door Premium.
stem: What is the main problem with that choice for Northline?
options: SSE needs a WebSocket upgrade, which Front Door's WAF blocks
SSE only works in the React Native app, not in browsers
Front Door does not support server-sent events, so the stream cannot run through it
SSE requires the SignalR client library on every page
explanation: Front Door's current documentation states it does not support SSE, and Northline routes everything public through it. SSE is a normal HTTP response, not a WebSocket upgrade, so the WAF-blocking idea misreads how it works.

scenario: The Node API on App Service needs to push order updates to customers through Azure SignalR Service, and the team does not want to run an ASP.NET Core app.
options: Default mode, with the Node API connecting to the service as the hub server
Classic mode, so the service picks hub or serverless behaviour per connection
Default mode, with the hub hosted on Azure Front Door
Serverless mode, with a negotiate Function issuing tokens and Functions or the REST API sending messages
explanation: Serverless mode needs no hub server: a negotiate Function hands out the URL and token, and Functions bindings or the REST API send to users and groups. Default mode expects an ASP.NET Core (or ASP.NET) hub server, which a Node API cannot be, and Classic is for old apps only.

stem: A contractor's live chat runs on a self-hosted Socket.IO server and is about to need a Redis adapter to scale beyond one instance. Which Azure service is the most direct move?
options: Azure SignalR Service in Default mode
Web PubSub for Socket.IO
Azure Notification Hubs
Azure Event Grid with webhook subscriptions
explanation: Web PubSub for Socket.IO is generally available and keeps the Socket.IO programming model with a few lines of change, removing the need for an adapter. SignalR Service is tempting because it is also real-time, but it speaks the SignalR protocol, so the chat would have to be rewritten.

stem: Which statement about SignalR Service and Web PubSub units on Standard and Premium is correct?
options: Each unit holds 1,000 concurrent connections and includes 1 million outbound messages a day
Each unit holds 20 connections, and messages are free without limit
Each unit holds 1,000 connections, and both inbound and outbound messages are billed from the first one
Units are billed per connection-minute, so idle connections cost nothing
explanation: A Standard or Premium unit gives 1,000 concurrent connections and 1 million included messages a day; only outbound messages count, in 2 KB chunks, and extras are billed per million. Twenty connections is the Free tier's single unit, and units are billed per day, not per connection-minute.

scenario: A stock-level push goes to a product group every second. On Black Friday, 5,000 people have that product page open all day.
stem: What is the most sensible fix?
options: Move to Premium, because Premium does not bill extra messages
Switch the product page back to polling every second
Batch stock changes to at most one push every few seconds per product, because each push is billed once per viewer
Send the stock update to each viewer's user ID instead of to the group
explanation: Each broadcast to the group is billed once per connection, so one push a second to 5,000 viewers is 18 million messages an hour; throttling cuts that directly. Sending per user creates exactly the same number of outbound messages, and Premium bills extra messages just like Standard.

stem: How should the negotiate endpoint decide which customer a real-time connection belongs to?
options: Accept the user ID the app sends in the negotiate request body, since the app has already signed the customer in
Let each client join an order-<id> group by name so it receives only its own order
Use the SignalR access key in the mobile app so the client can sign its own token
Validate the customer's External ID token and set the user ID on the server from its claims
explanation: The connection token is the connection's identity, so it must come from a validated sign-in token with the user ID set by the server. A client-supplied user ID or freely joinable group lets anyone read another customer's order, and an access key in an app bundle hands out the keys to the service.

scenario: Leo notices that after the train leaves a tunnel, the app reconnects but still shows "preparing" for an order that was dispatched while it was offline.
options: Increase the automatic reconnect delays so the client waits for a stable network
Refetch the order's current status from the API after every reconnect, and treat pushes as hints
Keep the WebSocket open while the app is in the background so nothing is ever missed
Route the WebSocket through Front Door so it buffers messages during the drop
explanation: Messages sent while a SignalR client is disconnected are lost, so the API must stay the source of truth and the app must refetch on reconnect. Holding a socket open in the background does not work reliably because the operating system suspends the app; push notifications cover that case, and Front Door does not buffer WebSocket messages.
